item.title: How 'fire-generated thunderstorms' make wildfires more deadly
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2350xnl4j5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How 'fire-generated thunderstorms' make wildfires more deadly - Published Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated from Bordeaux's surrounding region of Gironde, as France continues to fight against wildfires being stoked by an unprecedented "pyrocumulonimbus" or fire clouds. Scientists sometimes describe these clouds as a fire-generated thunderstorm because the fire itself provides the energy needed to build the cloud. The huge amount of heat generated by wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere. As the air rises, it cools and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a towering cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms. Turbulent winds created by the fire clouds can send embers shooting off in all directions, making wildfires unpredictable and harder to fight. Lightning strikes can also spark more blazes. French firefighting authorities have blamed the phenomenon for the blazes near Bordeaux, adding that it had never before been seen in the country. Across Europe, the summer months have sweltered through intense, record-breaking heatwaves with minimal rain. This has meant regions have become dry and susceptible to wildfires which have been sparked in France, Spain and the UK. On Monday the Gironde prefecture said the situation remained "broadly stable" overnight. But efforts to tackle the blaze could get further complicated with another heatwave forecast later this week with highs of up to 40C (104F) predicted in France this week. The wildfire in Gironde will likely burn "for many weeks" and could take months to fully extinguish, a senior official involved in the response has warned. Pyrocumulonimbus are more likely when there are extremely dangerous conditions such as high temperatures, strong winds and little moisture. Scientists have predicted that climate change is likely to increase the chances of such events. While once seen as fairly rare events, a similar example was seen during the 2019-2020 Black Summer bushfires in Australia, which created extreme "firestorms" that made its own weather. The event was one of the most intense and catastrophic fire seasons for the country, with at least 33 people killed - including four firefighters - and more than 11 million hectares (110,000 sq km or 27.2 million acres) of bush, forest and parks across Australia burnt. Fire officials in New South Wales reported that embers from the storm were landing 18 miles (30km) ahead of the front which was three times more than the usual distance. At the time, Nasa described pyrocumulonimbus as "the fire-breathing dragon of clouds, external" as they funnelled a smoke-like chimney into the earth's atmosphere while hurling thunderbolts, wind and rain. Similarly in California through the summer of 2021, the intense fires raging across the western United States generated pyrocumulonimbus. Smoky clouds towered a mile (1.6km) and rose over the blaze in California and surrounding states. California firefighting officials said at the time the season saw more than 7,300 wildfires burning across 1 million hectares (2.5 million acres) and at least three firefighters killed. item.title: Pirlo out of Italy football top job after backlash over Russian betting firm links
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g49r2338xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Pirlo out of Italy football top job after backlash over Russian betting firm links - Published Andrea Pirlo has said he is no longer a candidate to coach the Italian national side following days of controversy over his ties to a Russian betting company. His appointment as Italy's next head coach had not been confirmed by the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) yet was being treated as all but certain. But over the weekend several Italian politicians criticised the FIGC's choice, noting that Pirlo, 47, had taken up a role as global ambassador for Russia's Fonbet last October. The betting company has sponsored several sporting events involving veterans of Moscow's war in Ukraine and has organised events in Russia at which Pirlo appeared alongside pro-Kremlin figures. "Anyone who is or has been promoting Russia after 2022 should not hold national office," said Carlo Calenda of the centrist Azione party. "After learning last night that I am no longer a candidate for the Italian national team, I feel it is my duty to clarify some aspects," Pirlo, a former Internazionale, Juventus, AC Milan and Azzurri midfielder, wrote in an Instagram post on Monday morning. "Over the last few days I watched, with great bitterness, the debate that swirled around my name," he said, adding that any "professional collaboration" he undertook in his capacity as coach for United FC in Dubai "was exclusively of a commercial and sporting nature". "To assign a political meaning to that collaboration means ascribing to me beliefs which I have never expressed and that do not belong to me," Pirlo wrote. Pina Picierno, a vice-president of the European Parliament, said at the weekend that Italian football "desperately needed a cultural, ethical and managerial revolution" but that the choice of Pirlo "goes in the exact opposite direction". In contrast, Pirlo was offered support by the Russian ambassador in Rome, Aleksey Paramonov, who said that it was "saddening" to note that, "despite [Pirlo's] extraordinary contribution to world sport and to Italy's image around the world, in your own country, you are now being ostracized". Scrutiny of Pirlo's ties to Fonbet and Russia intensified last spring, when he took part in a Fonbet event held in Moscow, which saw him and former teammate Marco Materazzi sign autographs at Luzhniki Stadium. Nationalist pro-Kremlin pop star Shaman, who has repeatedly expressed his support for the Russian invasion of Ukraine, also performed at the event. At the time, Ukrainian skeleton slider Vladyslav Heraskevych - who was disqualified from the Winter Olympics over his helmet depicting fellow athletes killed in the war - noted the Luzhniki event had taken place on the same day as a large Russian attack on Ukraine. Heraskevych also criticised Pirlo for appearing next to Russian footballer Artem Dzyuba, who in the wake of the war in Ukraine posted on social media that he was "proud to be Russian". "It's sad to see childhood legends turn into moral bankrupts," Heraskevych said. The debate now risks engulfing new FIGC technical director Paolo Maldini, who has only been in post since 11 July and who Italian media say may resign over Pirlo's failed appointment. Maldini and his adviser, former AC Milan teammate Leonardo, were tasked with finding a new head coach to navigate Italy through a Nations League group that includes France, Belgium and Turkey in the autumn and then try to qualify for Euro 2028. The Italian football community has been undergoing much soul-searching after the team failed to qualify for a third World Cup earlier this year. Italy's loss on penalties to Bosnia-Herzegovina in April led to coach Gennaro Gattuso stepping down as well as a reshuffle of the FIGC echelons. Earlier this month, Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti were both unsuccessfully approached ahead of Pirlo. According to Italian media, other names currently being considered are Antonio Conte and Roberto Mancini - who led Italy to Euro 2020 glory before failing to qualify for the World Cup in Qatar and unceremoniously stepping down from the Italy bench to coach Saudi Arabia.

item.title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dng1v72lno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next? - Published In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct. So education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on Saturday, after more than a week of intense street protests, became a defining moment - one many young people celebrated as a rare victory. In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests". Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit. Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years". On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times. Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram." The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal. The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families. Initially, the protest drew little attention. That changed on 18 July when Delhi police forcibly removed and hospitalised hunger-striking educator Sonam Wangchuk. Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them. The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country. Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed. Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning". "For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says. Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage. Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded. "Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says. Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture. India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data. Even graduates are struggling: a 2026 Azim Premji University study found fewer than 7% of jobseekers secured permanent salaried work within a year, and fewer than 4% landed white-collar jobs. The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year. On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended. "I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices." Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over." A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next". But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension. Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees". But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations. Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40. Human Rights Watch says, external that under Modi, Indian authorities have "routinely prosecuted activists, journalists, and peaceful protesters on fabricated counterterrorism and hate speech laws". Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual". At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".

item.title: Musk takes 'crusade' to Europe with Armie Hammer film
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y4w5nwk00o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Musk takes 'crusade' to Europe with Armie Hammer film - Published An American vigilante tears across an unnamed European country, killing dozens of police officers and judges, slaughtering a gang of rapists, and killing a refugee family and a random civilian – all in the name of a crusade against Muslim migrants and "woke" government officials. Citizen Vigilante, a film from German director Uwe Boll and starring actor Armie Hammer, is violent – and very schlocky – stuff. Initially denied a rating by German's film regulator, it would likely have garnered very little attention, had it not caught the eye of the world's richest person. Elon Musk made the film free to view via his social media platform X for 48 hours in late June, and the subsequent attention briefly pushed the movie into the top of the charts of several streaming providers including Apple and Amazon. At one point he reposted a message about the film that described vigilante murder as the "moderate response" to violent crimes committed by immigrants. It's just one of many recent examples of the tech titan's increasing interest in extreme ideas and activists, and in particular his support of political parties and politicians on the right in Europe. Musk left the Trump administration more than a year ago and his Doge project, which aimed to slash the size of the US federal government, has since been wound down. But he has recently sought to conquer other political territory. "This is a crusade," says Georgios Samaras, an assistant professor of public policy at King's College London who studies the European and US far right. "Musk uses the power he has to amplify the ideas that he thinks should dominate society. He knows he has the money and he knows he has the influence." 'Radicalised by his own network' Much of that influence comes via X, formerly Twitter, the social media platform that Musk bought outright in 2022. Since stripping away many of the old Twitter's content moderation rules - derided as censorship by Musk and others - the network has become a haven for far-right beliefs and conspiracy theories. In turn, X appears to have shaped Musk. Although it's difficult to glean a cohesive worldview from social media fragments - Musk did not respond to requests for comment for this story - his output has demonstrated a growing obsession with race and white people in particular. He has posted and reposted a slew of messages - often from white nationalist and far-right activists - portraying white people as under threat, including messages like "Whites are a rapidly dying minority" and "If White men become a minority, we will be slaughtered". He has endorsed the leader of France's hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen. "She is France's last hope," he wrote. Musk also recently reposted a video from the far-right activist Tommy Robinson that suggested police are going easy on criminals if they have brown skin, with the comment "literally true". He's also boosted right-wing politicians and parties in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and the UK. Although at one point he toyed with donating huge sums of money to Reform UK, he since broke with Nigel Farage over Farage's shunning of Robinson, and more recently has boosted the profile of Rupert Lowe's breakaway party Restore Britain – a Reform rival that seeks to take an even tougher line on immigration. In June, after a Sudanese man was accused of a brutal stabbing in Northern Ireland, Musk shared a list of street protest locations posted by Robinson, adding: "Only by protesting REPEATEDY and LOUDLY will there be any change!!" In other posts he claimed that former Prime Minister Keir Starmer "hates white people" and shared an image of the stabbing suspect with the comment "millions must go". Mobs rioted on the streets of Belfast, where the stabbing happened. Police highlighted the role of social media in co-ordinating the disorder. The Center for Countering Digital Hate, a research and advocacy group that has been the target of legal action by Musk in the past, tallied 4,000 calls for violence on X written as responses underneath posts by Musk, Lowe and Robinson. "Many people on the right use Musk as a means to an end," says AJA Woods, a historian studying conspiracy theories and reactionary politics. "He's seen as a source of funds, or someone who's in control of X so can be used to promote their ideas… he's a convenient ally." When contacted for comment, Lowe described the CCDH report as "embarrassing guff" and called the BBC a "disgrace". Remigration exported Despite being in charge of several enormous companies, Musk regularly wades into ostensibly local disputes, not just in Belfast but across Europe, apparently gleaning much of his knowledge from people he follows on X. "You find a tutoring relationship, one in which Musk is inducted into their talking points," says Ben Tarnoff, co-author of Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed. One of those talking points is his embrace of the term "remigration". Anti-immigration advocates use it to refer to mass deportations, even of legal migrants. In its extreme form, it means the removal through force or heavy persuasion of all non-whites or foreigners, even if they were born in or and have deep roots in their home countries. Slightly more moderate versions focus on recent migrants or those not fully integrated into European societies. The concept has been linked to violent activity, experts say, and Musk and X have not only been instrumental in spreading the idea across Europe, but in importing it to the United States, Tarnoff says. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees US immigration, posted an X message consisting of one word: "Remigrate". "Something that Musk shares with members of the American right and particularly with Donald Trump's circle is a view of Europe and the UK as the ancestral home of white civilisation, but a home that has surrendered itself to the woke forces of multiculturalism," says Tarnoff. - What we know so far about the Berlin Pride ramming attack - Published22 hours ago
Saturday's attack at a Berlin Pride event - which was described by officials as an "Islamist terror attack" - gave far-right influencers that Musk converses with on X another opportunity to warn of civilizational collapse and call for drastic measures in response. Musk later wrote in response to a Spanish anti-immigration influencer: "Anyone who opposes remigration is a traitor". 'Astonishingly bad' and 'fascist propaganda' Citizen Vigilante was cheered by many far-right activists on X, even as others slammed the movie, not only for its politics but for its thin plot, cheap-looking special effects and abundance of gore. After the publicity boost, Boll estimated that the film made about $600,000 from streaming, against a budget of $2m. Critics were scathing. Variety called it "astonishingly bad" while prominent American conservative commentator Rod Dreher called it "fascist propaganda", although he and some others on the right defended its depiction of a Europe in turmoil. The film's portrayal of European society dovetails with the bleak vision pushed by Musk and others on the right – that citizens have been utterly betrayed by a corrupt establishment, that migrants are at the root of violence and chaos, and that extreme measures are needed to restore order. "People who are complaining that he spends the first half of the movie murdering white people not migrants fail to understand… Always hang a traitor before you shoot an enemy," read one message reposted by Musk. - 'Let's enjoy the ride' of AI, Musk tells The Economist - Published4 days ago
Challenged last week in an Economist interview on whether he was being irresponsible to promote a film which glorifies the murder of a Muslim family, Musk said: "It's a movie and it's worth watching." "I don't think Europe's a hell hole," he said, but also insisted that "there was out of control rape and murder." He also stood by previous statements that he believed civil war in the UK was "inevitable", and referring to Muslims, he said: "If you have a large and rapidly growing group of people whose beliefs are antithetical to Western beliefs, at some point there will be a reckoning." The tech titan also said he had not visited the UK in several years. Musk's defenders have often praised his professed support for unfettered online speech and have chalked some of his more extreme stances up to online exaggeration. Others say his influence over politics in the UK and Europe is limited. "I don't think he has much political sway in Britain or on the continent," says Gawain Towler, a former Reform UK director of communications who still supports the party. Towler says he credits Musk with highlighting rape gangs in British cities and says he is relaxed about the tycoon's support for Lowe and Restore. "I generally prefer the stuff he says about his businesses," he says. Related topics - Published3 September 2025

item.title: The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0m8z6de3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold - Published The reigning 57kg world champion boxer Jaismine Lamboria from India throws punches for a living, but when it comes to handling pressure, she looks to one of her country's most celebrated cricketing legends for inspiration. "I really admire MS Dhoni's mindset," says the soft-spoken Lamboria of the former Indian captain. "He is known as 'Captain Cool' for a reason, and I want to be calm like him." That composure will be particularly valuable for Lamboria over the coming days. The 24-year-old is one of India's strongest boxing gold-medal prospects at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, looking to improve on the bronze she won at Birmingham 2022. Coming off a breakout 2025 during which she won World Cup golds in Astana and Delhi before becoming world champion in Liverpool, Lamboria is in Glasgow with an uncomplicated ambition. "I aim to change the colour of that medal to gold," she says. "That's what I've been training and preparing towards." At 5ft 8½in, Lamboria is tall by Indian boxing standards. Her Olympic debut in Paris ended in a first-round defeat to Tokyo silver medallist Nesthy Petecio of the Philippines. But the setback came in the weight class she had only recently returned to. After spending nearly three years boxing at 60kg, Lamboria dropped back to 57kg during the Paris qualification campaign - a move that ultimately paid off when she won the world title by defeating Paris Olympic silver medallist Julia Atena Szeremeta of Poland. "That Paris 2024 Olympics exit was disappointing but it was an eye-opener," says Lamboria. "It prompted several changes in me - physically and mentally. And a significant part of it has come about at the Army Sports Institute (ASI) in Pune, which is where I train." Lamboria credits her ASI coaches for improving his physical strength and a motivational coach and sports psychologist for sharpening her mental game. The Indian Army, however, has provided the wider institutional framework around much of her development. After winning bronze at the 2022 Commonwealth Games, Lamboria became the first female boxer inducted into the army, joining the Corps of Military Police. She now trains under its Mission Olympics Wing. "It's a great honour they wanted to begin with me, but I also see it as an opportunity to become a role model for female athletes," says Lamboria of joining a system that has produced Olympians and Paralympians, including Olympic javelin champion Neeraj Chopra. In early 2024, the Indian Army launched the Girls Sports Company to train girls aged 12 to 16 in four Olympic sports, including boxing, creating a pathway to elite competition and army recruitment. "These girl athletes are doing very well too," says Lamboria. "One boxer has already won Asian Championships gold, which makes me really happy. I may have been the first female boxer in the Indian Army, but I won't be the last." Lamboria's relationship with boxing, however, began long before the army entered her story. Born in the northern state of Haryana, she grew up in Bhiwani, a city synonymous with Indian boxing and widely nicknamed the country's 'Mini Cuba'. Her great-grandfather Hawa Singh was one of Indian boxing's early giants. A heavyweight, he won successive Asian Games gold medals in 1966 and 1970 and was among those who established the famed Bhiwani Boxing Club, which would later produce boxers including Olympic medallist Vijender Singh. Even so, it is not Hawa's medals that feature most prominently in the stories Lamboria remembers hearing about him at home. "He was powerful, but there was also so much humility in him," she says. Her earliest boxing influences were her uncles, Sandeep Singh and Parvinder Singh. "I grew up watching them compete," she says. "They were the ones who got me started." Lamboria began boxing seriously around the age of 14, training first at an academy run by Hawa's son, Sanjay Sheoran, before continuing under her uncles. Though the sport ran through her extended family, Lamboria grew up in a household of modest means. Her father, Jaiveer, works as a home guard, while her mother, Joginder, is a homemaker. "Their support has been a big reason why I was the first girl in my immediate family to take up sport seriously," she says, "not least as the youngest among the girls in the family." Her inspirations, meanwhile, extend well beyond her own family. Lamboria grew up idolising Olympic medallists MC Mary Kom and Vijender Singh. Later, she looked up to Indian Army boxers Amit Panghal and Manish Kaushik, Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, American swimming great Michael Phelps and Indian sprinting legend Milkha Singh. Closer to home, she credits senior Indian boxers Nikhat Zareen, Lovlina Borgohain and Pooja Rani, not just for their medals but for the encouragement they offer younger athletes. "When you look at them, you naturally feel that you want to do what they have done," she says. Now, Lamboria is beginning to occupy that role herself. "For a long time, boxing has been seen as a male-dominated sport," she says. "Being a woman boxer and an Army athlete, it means a lot to compete on the world stage, prove myself and inspire others through my performances." That change is reflected in the Commonwealth Games too. Boxing has been part of the event since 1930, but women's competition was introduced only in 2014. In Glasgow, bouts began on 24 July, with the finals on 31 July and 1 August. After winning bronze in Birmingham four years ago, Lamboria hopes to leave Glasgow with gold. "When you're competing overseas and the national anthem plays, it's a completely different feeling," she says. "I experienced that at the World Championships in Liverpool last year. That's the moment I want to recreate here."

Watch: Protesters celebrate resignation of India's education minister Protesters in India are celebrating after the resignation of the country's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands of young people had been demonstrating in Delhi, demanding Pradhan resign after exam paper leaks and testing irregularities. Now Pradhan has resigned, the protests organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been called off. CJP is a national movement born out of a satirical campaign, rather than an actual party, and has faced heavy police crackdowns.
